title: Show HN: Cerea – yet another self-hosted LLM chat front end
text:
Here is Cerea, a self-hostable, open-source (Apache 2.0) chat+agent frontend for LLMs. It works alone with any OpenAI-compatible inference provider, but it's way better when coupled with the model gateway I'm also developing, Pystino (https://github.com/paoloviviani/Pystino).

I came to this after struggling to find a hosted chat interface that was truly open source, that I really enjoyed to use, and that was simple enough to be shared and used by family. In particular, I was looking for something that could provide the smooth and integrated user experience of commercial products for the tasks needed by family (e.g., document editing, form filling, notes and knowledge management), but backed by open models hosted wherever I decide.

Then it became richer, now supporting: remote coding agents (wrapping Opencode), delegation and coordination between agents, integration between chat/projects and code agents (this one to me is a pain point for Claude, which I use at work), projects, RAG, rich artifacts support, schedules, and more.

You can try it yourself, either cloning the full repo and head to Cerea/kit, or just the deploy kit with a script (https://github.com/paoloviviani/Cerea#quick-start).

It's just a docker compose with a ./configure script that helps to generate a sensible .env for the specific scenario. It works in the browser and as a PWA on mobile.

I hope you'll enjoy, feel free to reach out for questions.
author: pviviani

title: Re: Watchdeck: See what every Claude Code session was ...
text:
watchdeck shows every Claude Code session on your machine as a live map: every tool call, who decided it (your deny rules, Claude Code's auto check, you, the OS sandbox), and what was stopped. A denial becomes a rule in one click, written into Claude Code's own settings, so the next session never asks again. Local, private, one binary; nothing leaves your machine.

Why I built it: Claude Code's own controls are good, but each decision lives inside one session and disappears with it. I wanted one place that keeps every decision across sessions and projects, shows me what needs a rule, and writes that rule where Claude Code reads it. Where Claude Code has no control at all, scripts that skills run, MCP servers, named commands, watchdeck runs them in an OS sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) with no network and no access to credential paths unless you grant it.

What it does, concretely:

- A dashboard (`watchdeck` opens it): Home says whether you are protected and what needs you; Sessions is the map of every session, live, with a timeline per session; Rules is everything that limits an agent on this machine, strongest first, with an add sheet that previews the file it will write. - A hook on Bash and the file tools that adds a few milliseconds per call (median 6.2 ms on my M-series Mac in the runs before the v0.1.0 tag, measured before every release and checked in CI). - Leak watch: if a secret-shaped string shows up in a tool result or a reply, Home tells you where, never the secret itself. - `watchdeck doctor --prove` runs the hook you installed against a built-in canary in a throwaway HOME and reports five checks, so "it is enforced" is something you can see.

What it does not do, up front: it cannot stop prose. A `SKILL.md` can still talk the model into misusing Read or WebFetch; only scripts are sandboxed. Network is on or off per subject; no hostname filtering yet. In my own headless study (18 sessions, three models, three scenarios), no planted marker leaked, but three WebFetch calls went around a refused `curl` untouched, so I added rules that cover every route to a host or a path with one intent. macOS is verified end to end; Linux passes CI but has not run on a developer machine. No Windows.

Releases are reproducible, signed (keyless cosign bundle), attested (GitHub build provenance), with an SBOM per archive, and the installer can verify all of that before it installs anything. Apache-2.0.

Install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panda-Taps-LLC/watchdeck/m... | sh` or `brew install Panda-Taps-LLC/tap/watchdeck`, then `watchdeck setup`. Remove it with `watchdeck uninstall`.

The ask: tell me what you see on your machine that it should have caught, and what rule you wanted that it could not write. I will answer every issue.

title: Re: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at A...
text:
> The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted.

Of note, "the acceleration in late 2025" believe has to do with Opus 4.5 which in my view and from Metr's analysis[0], was the point where their tests stopped working because the model was so good that doing work without using it took much more time.

> We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.... We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.

In a mini bet, I'd say that Anthropic is going to win by a large margin in what's going on. I've used the other models and no matter what the benchmarks are, places like OpenAI, Gemini, or the Deepseek / Kimi models haven't come close to the ability of the Claude models and harness. If what they say in this post is right, with "We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress.", this could be a sort of game over for the other models.

Even with Opus 5.5 in the past month and a half has been a changer in its abilities. In my dev process, I can give it much more freedom and trust with the workflows and connections I have to do the valid work to where I can do more, bigger tasks at once. I can't tell you how curious I am with the Opus 5.6 and whatever Model 4 is going to be called (along with the cost!) will do for dev work. And if this keeps increasing, and if there are subtle tricks that Anthropic has that the other companies don't, what that means for finding solutions and overall value and if the others are ever going to be able to catch up in any way.

All speculation, but what a time to be a dev in these times and get the first hand experience of all of this!

[0] https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/#wider-adopti...

title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits
text:
I’ve been doing a lot of solo development lately and found myself hitting Claude token limits halfway through the week constantly. Even with a Max plan, I’d have to switch over to Codex or Cursor, and it would be a bit difficult to get used to the nuances of each harness.

It’s still a problem for me, but I finally built Thinker to save me some tokens and help me get a bit more out of my coding agent subscriptions.

I started off a bit in the dark about how token billing works, and had to dig deeper to figure out what workflows ended up hurting my budget the most. By far, it was large context windows. Claude tries to help out on costs by offering prompt caching - which is sort of a bandage on the bigger problem: context bloat.

I find that my context window gets bloated with unneeded tokens in two main ways:

Tool outputs from subtasks that are long finished. File reads, Bash commands, MCP outputs, etc. Main idea is that the model finished the work but carries the weight of it for every subsequent call - translating to wasted token usage. CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md getting way too big. Lots of content gets dumped into these files as your agents work in your repo. I found that it’s not clear what is actually useful to be included there. Every token here counts, because it will be paid for in every session, and its cost scales linearly with the duration of your session.

Thinker addresses both of these issues. We have a proxy that wires in between your harness and model to cut out old context that we determine is no longer needed for your current task. Based on the provider you’re using, we determine the right time to batch enough context to cut that justifies the cache re-write cost, which gets paid off after X subsequent calls.

We also analyze your sessions and figure out which parts of your instruction files don’t really get used - and send you suggestions to cut or compress those sections. Thinker will kick off a subagent to do that work for you and open a PR you can review.

Finally, we use your sessions to record knowledge notes by distilling your sessions with a cheap model (Haiku, Luna). These notes are then served at prompt time via a cross-encoder, also on your machine, that decides whether a note is relevant to the user’s prompt.

Here are some data points to show how exactly Thinker saves you coding agent costs: https://thinker.sh/see-the-data

If you’re hitting problems at all with usage limits, it’d be great to hear how you’ve been trying to mitigate it.

Our open-source repo here (MIT License): https://github.com/yoavshmariahu/thinker

title: Show HN: Lunar – a coding harness built for transparency and efficiency
text:
Hi everyone,

I built Lunar to make my day to day work on our AI gateway easier: basic testing of different providers, advanced testing of features like complexity router, and so on. Lunar allows you to easily switch across providers, gives you debugging tools (`/debug` to dump provider response headers, `/request` to dump the current prompt as a curl request, easy configuration with Lua, and more...).

You can use your OpenAI or xAI subscription on it (Anthropic also supported, but use it at your own risk, as it's against Anthropic's terms - I developed it as an experimente). API keys also supported.

Eager to know your thoughts! :)

title: Re: My psychophysics as a bilateral cochlear implant u...
text:
Author here. I'm Korean, and I have cochlear implants in both ears, which I received in a clinical trial in 2025. No one could tell me what I actually hear, so between 11 October and 4 November 2026 I ran seven psychophysical tests on myself (10,992 trials), using browser test apps that Claude built for me. I'm an amateur, so there are surely mistakes, and corrections are very welcome.

All trial-level data, the analysis code and Lean 4 checks of the apps' logic are on GitHub (non-commercial licenses): https://github.com/mi-rae-lab/ci-psychophysics-data

I do not speak English. The page was translated with Claude, and I will use AI to read and answer replies, so my answers may be slow.

title: Show HN: Securing GrokBot
text:
A friend at another tech startup was telling me how they started using Grok Bot and loved it. Surprise surprise they also got pretty worried about what it's doing and the visibility they had.

Digging under the hood, hey there's a Linux VM and a Chrome browser. This is really cool because it essentially defines an environment that is really similar to a typical workstation.

After some playing around I got the LimaCharlie EDR installed, the Chrome LC EDR installed and the email provider connected to the LC Email Security. Took a few iteration to make it all smooth but it works great on the free community edition!

So you get to see what is executing on the box, where the bot is browsing and emails in and out. I built a couple detections using AI and just made it a doc in our documentation so you can just tell Grok Bot:

""" Secure my Grok Bot with LimaCharlie by following https://docs.limacharlie.io/grok-bot/ """

The TL;DR; of what it does: - all of it goes to your own private tenant - installs a linux EDR on the box - installs a Chrome extension that is essentially an EDR in your browser - if you want, connects your gmail (any IMAP is supported really) and is like an EDR for the email - If you want it sends the alerts to your Grok Bot (I'm curious to see the advantage of a feedback loop here), or it's available on the web app.limacharlie.io

The other option I left in was to leave the CLI authenticated on the Grok Bot. The interesting bit about that is that because the CLI has 100% coverage of the platform, you can ask the Grok Bot to start setting up new alerts, investigate alerts, configure everything...

I tried to make it more generic for other AI agents where I have no idea what the environment is: https://docs.limacharlie.io/2-sensors-deployment/tutorials/s... though disclaimer I have not tried it yet, but it's not rocket science and more frontier AI models are now rocket scientists.

The advantage that Grok Bot has is that it fundamentally allows things to execute on the VM and talk out. The other ones (Muse, Dots) seem to proxy every single thing and generally be extremely difficult to extend.

Anyway, hope it helps some of you! (and yes, got it to make a cool video :D) https://youtu.be/yZZuBgKWd1k
